record.prompt: How could a small local museum make repeat visits worthwhile with a tiny budget and no new permanent exhibits? Develop practical, distinct directions.

nodes.body:
**Title: The Rotating "Micro-Lens" Strategy**

**Core Idea:** Change the narrative perspective monthly (e.g., "Objects as Tools" vs. "Objects as Failures"), rewriting labels and adding one cheap, thematic object.

**Example:** Shift from "Town History" to "Sound and Silence," using old photos to discuss ambient noise, paired with a single donated, broken radio.

**Tradeoff:** Requires significant staff time for constant re-labeling and curatorial writing, risking burnout if not carefully scheduled.

How could a small local museum make repeat visits worthwhile with a tiny budget and no new permanent exhibits? Develop practical, distinct directions.

**Title: The Rotating "Micro-Lens" Strategy

**Core Idea:** Instead of adding objects, change the narrative perspective. Rotate the primary interpretive lens (e.g., "Objects as Tools," "Objects as Artifacts of Failure") every month, rewriting labels and adding one new, cheaply sourced object that supports the new theme.

**Example:** A local history museum shifts from a standard "Town History" view to a "Sound and Silence" theme, using old photographs to discuss ambient noise levels, paired with a single donated, broken radio.

**Tradeoff:** Requires significant staff time for constant re-labeling and curatorial writing, risking burnout if not carefully scheduled.

nodes.title: The 4-Week "Limited Run" Rotation
nodes.summary: Core Idea: Treat existing artifacts as a live theater cast. Every four weeks, re-hang a small cluster of 5–10 items into a new, thematic micro-exhibit
nodes.body:
**Title: The 4-Week "Limited Run" Rotation**

**Core Idea:** Treat existing artifacts as a live theater cast. Every four weeks, re-hang a small cluster of 5–10 items into a new, thematic micro-exhibit. Market it as a "Limited Run" with a specific end date to create urgency, forcing visitors to return before the "show" closes.

**Example:** A local history museum creates a "Secrets of the Main Street" 4-week run using only existing documents and photos. Each month, the "plot" changes (e.g., "The Great Fire," "The Prohibition Era"), requiring only new label cards and minor rearrangement.

**Tradeoff:** This strategy relies heavily on consistent marketing to drive each new "opening." If the community misses the announcement, the urgency factor fails, and the rotation becomes just a static display.
